name: Verifiable Credential
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Digital Proof Without Digital Oversharing
lesson.summary: A verifiable credential is a tamper-evident, digitally signed claim, like a diploma or a license, that lets a holder prove facts about themselves to a verifier while often disclosing only the minimum necessary.
lesson.body:
A verifiable credential, standardized by the W3C, is a digital version of the paper credentials people already carry: a diploma, a driver's license, a professional certification, a proof of employment. Three roles are involved. An issuer, a university, a government agency, an employer, creates the credential and digitally signs it with its private key, exactly the mechanism covered in Digital Signature: a cryptographic guarantee that this specific issuer created this specific claim and that it has not been altered since. A holder, the individual the credential is about, stores it in a digital wallet. A verifier, a bar checking age or an employer checking a degree, checks the credential's signature against the issuer's known public key to confirm authenticity, without needing to call the issuer directly.

What makes verifiable credentials more than just a signed PDF is their connection to zero-knowledge proofs. A well designed credential system lets the holder prove one specific fact drawn from the credential without handing over the entire document. If a bar needs to know a patron is over twenty-one, an old-fashioned driver's license discloses the exact birthdate, the home address, the license number, a photo, and often more, far more than the bar actually needs. A verifiable credential built with selective disclosure techniques can instead let the holder prove the single statement that the holder of this signed credential is over twenty-one, without revealing the birthdate or any other field. This is the password example from the last chapter, applied to identity documents: proving a fact is true without revealing the underlying data that makes it true.

A concrete example: mobile driver's licenses now being rolled out in several jurisdictions, along with elements of the EU's digital identity framework, are built on exactly this pattern. Another common case is a university issuing digitally signed diploma credentials, so a graduate's future employer can verify the degree instantly and cryptographically, without emailing a registrar's office and waiting days for confirmation, and without the graduate needing to expose an entire academic transcript just to prove they hold one specific degree.

The broader significance is that a verifiable credential replaces calling the issuer to check with verifying the signature yourself, the same shift a blockchain makes for transaction history, applied instead to personal claims. The next two chapters build the surrounding identity infrastructure, decentralized identifiers and self-sovereign identity, that let holders manage and present these credentials without depending on any single centralized identity provider.
